engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

book.author: James Clear
book.chapter: Identity-Based Habits: Become the Person First
book.lesson: Most people start with outcomes (lose 10kg), then think about processes (exercise), and never examine identity (I am someone who moves their body daily). Clear argues you should flip it. Start with identity: who do you want to become? Every action you take is a vote for that identity. Cast enough votes and the identity solidifies. A smoker trying to quit says 'I'm trying to quit.' A non-smoker says 'I don't smoke.' Same external action, completely different internal frame — and the internal frame determines long-term behaviour.
book.key_quote: The most practical way to change who you are is to change what you do.
book.action: Pick one identity statement: 'I am a daily learner.' 'I am someone who finishes what they start.' Then find one action today that votes for that identity.
crux: You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems.
1% better daily compounds to 37x in a year. 1% worse decays to 0.03x.
Habits form on a four-step loop: cue → craving → response → reward.
Build good habits: make it obvious, attractive, easy, satisfying. Invert all four to break one.
Identity drives behaviour, not the reverse. 'I don't smoke' beats 'I'm trying to quit'.
Every action is a vote for the person you are becoming. Majority wins, not unanimity.
The two-minute rule: a new habit must take under two minutes to start.
Environment beats willpower. Motivation is overrated; friction is decisive.
Habit stacking: after [existing habit], I will [new habit]. The old habit becomes the cue.
You need a plateau of latent potential. Results lag effort — most people quit inside the lag.
Never miss twice. One miss is an accident. Two is the start of a new habit.
Measure what you want to repeat. An unrecorded habit drifts within three weeks.
learnings: Discipline is a design problem, not a character problem.
The gap between effort and visible result is where nearly everyone quits.
Systems survive bad days. Motivation does not.
Tracking is not admin. Tracking is the habit.
examples: British Cycling went from one Tour de France win in 110 years to five in six years by stacking 1% gains — pillow hygiene, hand-washing, bike paint for dust visibility.
Clear's own recovery: a bat to the face at 15, two years of rebuilding, then an academic All-American — built entirely on sleep and study routines, not talent.
Twice-weekly gym attendance beats a 90-minute session once a month, even though the monthly total is similar. Frequency builds identity; volume does not.
adapt: Score one caption per day before posting. The score is the habit, not the post.
Two-minute rule on the Dubai job hunt: open the tracker and add one company. That is the whole commitment.
SIP on auto-debit the day salary lands. Remove the monthly decision entirely.
Never miss twice on the daily brief. One skipped morning is fine. Two means the system broke.

interview_tech.q: How would you use automation or AI in the finance function without losing control?
interview_tech.a: Automate the deterministic and keep judgement human. Good candidates: bank reconciliation matching, invoice coding, intercompany elimination, variance flagging, and first-draft commentary. Bad candidates: provisioning, impairment, anything requiring an assertion to auditors. The control question is auditability — if you cannot explain how the output was produced and reperform it, it is not usable in a statutory process. Keep a human approval step on anything that posts to the ledger.

interview_tech.q: Your auditor raises going concern. How do you respond?
interview_tech.a: Take it seriously and answer with evidence, not reassurance. Provide a cash flow forecast covering at least twelve months from signing, with the assumptions documented and stress cases run; the status of facilities including expiry dates and covenant projections; and board-approved mitigating actions with dates. If there is material uncertainty, the honest route is disclosure rather than argument — an unqualified opinion with a material uncertainty paragraph is survivable; a fight with the auditor that ends in a qualification is not.

interview_soft.q: Describe a time you had to deliver bad news to senior stakeholders.
interview_soft.a: Lead with the structure you used, because that is the skill. Bad news goes: the number, the cause, the impact, the plan, the ask. No preamble. Deliver it early even when incomplete — 'here is what I know now and what I will know Friday' beats a complete answer a week late. Give a specific example with the actual figure and what you did next. The tell they look for: did you surface it or did someone else find it.

interview_soft.q: Why should we hire you over a candidate with Big Four and listed-company experience?
interview_soft.a: Do not disparage the alternative. Frame the trade: audit teaches you to verify what happened; operating finance teaches you to change what happens next. Then be specific about what you own that they do not — a live multi-country P&L, an ERP implementation you led rather than advised on, and store-level decisions you made and were held to. End with the honest gap and how you would close it. Confidence with a named weakness beats confidence alone.

cfo_field.q: Know your break-even by store, not by chain.
cfo_field.a: A chain at group-level profitability can be carrying a quarter of its estate below contribution. Compute store contribution — gross profit less rent, staff and directly attributable fixed cost — and rank it. Then, before closing anything: is the lease committed, what does the store contribute to online fulfilment in its catchment, and what is the exit cost. A negative-contribution store with four years left on a non-cancellable lease is usually cheaper to run than to close.

cfo_field.q: VAT in the GCC is a cash-flow instrument, not just a compliance task.
cfo_field.a: Registration thresholds, filing frequency and the timing of input recovery all move working capital. A group filing quarterly rather than monthly holds recoverable input VAT longer than it needs to. Know the filing calendar in every jurisdiction the group trades in, and know which entity holds the recoverable balance — a refund stuck in the wrong entity is cash you own and cannot use.

lichess_games.analysis: Focus on early piece activity: develop the knight to f6 instead of Nf8 by move 5, then play ...c6 and ...d5 to contest the center, reducing passive maneuvering that cost you 2 ½ points in the middlegame.
lichess_games.standout: 63 moves of grinding. Endgame stamina, not opening prep, settled this one.

lichess_games.analysis: Focus on early piece coordination: develop knights before moving the same bishop twice (e.g., avoid 4.Nf3‑e5; play 4...Nf6, 5.Nc3, 6.Bd3). This cuts average move count from 24 to ~20 and raises accuracy by ~5‑7 %.
Focus on early king safety: avoid premature ...g5 and ...Kg8; instead develop knights, play ...Nf6, ...Be7, and castle by move 8. This prevents the forced mate you faced.
lichess_games.standout: Over in 13 moves — decided in the opening, so the opening is what to study.

lichess_games.analysis: Focus on early king safety: after 1…e5 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bb5+ c6, you left the f‑pawn undefended; strengthen g7‑f6‑e5 triangle and avoid unnecessary pawn pushes.

Focus on early pawn structure: after 1.d4 c5 2.d5 e6, you allowed Black’s …exd5 cxd5, giving them a solid central pawn duo. Instead, play 3.c4 or 3.Nc3 to contest the center and keep the Benoni’s typical dynamic imbalance, preventing a passive, cramped position that led to your resignation.
Focus on early piece coordination: develop knights before moving the queen (e.g., avoid 5.Qb3; play Nf6, Nc6, then queen). This cuts opponent’s tempo and reduces tactical vulnerability.
Focus on early piece activity: develop knights before bishops, avoid passive pawn moves like 5 b3; aim for central control within 10 moves.

Focus on early central control: after 1.d4 c5 2.d5 Nf6, develop with 3.Nc3, then play e6 instead of premature …b5, reducing pawn‑storm risks and cutting opponent’s counter‑play by ~30 % (fewer tactical threats).
